introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.opening: Arkansas does not lack ideas. We have spent generations arguing over ideas. What we lack is a common method for asking whether those ideas actually leave ordinary people more capable of building lives of their own choosing.
introduction.why_this_book: This book began with questions rather than a predetermined ideology. It asks what prosperity means for a household, how money moves, who builds capability, what must physically work, who holds power, and how a free people could change course without breaking what already works.
introduction.why_arkansas: Arkansas is specific enough to be honest and large enough to matter. A philosophy that cannot survive contact with one state's households, budgets, places, and politics does not deserve to lecture the country.
introduction.why_now: Pressure is rising on costs, capability, institutions, and trust. Waiting for a perfect national consensus is not a plan for the people living here now.
introduction.how_to_read: Read straight through if you can — Chapters 1 through 10 are one argument. Use the Reader's Contract early. Use Follow One Idea if you want a single thread. Use Understand / Learn / Prove when you want depth. And know this before you reach Chapter 9: we deliberately tried to destroy our own conclusions before publishing them.
introduction.unusual: We deliberately tried to destroy our own conclusions before publishing them.

promises: We will distinguish evidence from illustration.
We will tell you when something is unknown.
We will not count hypothetical public money.
We will distinguish aspiration from prediction.
We will change conclusions when evidence requires it.
readers_contract.closing: You do not have to agree with Constitutional Capitalism. Our responsibility is to make it understandable enough that you can decide for yourself.

afterword.title: Afterword — An Invitation
body: This book does not end with a request that you agree.
It ends with a request that you test it.
Ask who owns. Ask who decides. Ask who pays. Ask who benefits. Ask who bears the risk. Ask where the surplus goes. Ask what happens to the household. Ask what happens when the system fails.
Then demand the same rigor from Constitutional Capitalism itself.

definitions.short: Free people. Competitive markets. Distributed power. Broader ownership. Capable communities. Prosperity that compounds.
definitions.canonical: A market-based political-economic system that protects individual liberty, broadens the ability of households and communities to build capital, keeps economic and political power from capturing one another, uses government only within defined constitutional roles, and measures success by whether prosperity and productive capability compound across generations.

definitions.short: Households retaining more capability, ownership, security, time, and agency across a lifetime — not GDP alone.
definitions.canonical: The condition in which ordinary households can build lives of their own choosing with expanding capability over time.

definitions.short: What remains after essential costs when capability and ownership can compound.
definitions.canonical: The residual capacity for savings, ownership, resilience, and choice after meeting essential household costs.

definitions.short: Meaningful choices about the direction of a life, not dictated solely by immediate economic survival.
definitions.canonical: The ability to make meaningful choices without every decision being dictated by immediate economic survival.

definitions.short: What people can actually do — skills, health, knowledge, and the power to act.
definitions.canonical: Human capacity to learn, work, create, adapt, and participate — the primary productive capital of a society.

definitions.short: Whether a place keeps and grows the capability to create value — not merely keeps dollars from leaving.
definitions.canonical: The net change in a community's ability to produce, adapt, and earn — distinct from crude dollar-retention nationalism.

definitions.short: Shared capacity a place must keep functional to remain free and productive.
definitions.canonical: Infrastructure, institutions, and systems without which households and markets cannot reliably function.

definitions.short: Public capital committed only when gates for additionality, returns, and accountability pass.
definitions.canonical: Government capital deployed under constitutional constraints to create lasting productive value — never counted as COUNTABLE cash until proven.

definitions.short: $0 until alternative public cash is proven.
definitions.canonical: Proven alternative public cash available to spend or use for tax replacement. Until proven: $0.

definitions.short: When wealth or office converts into unaccountable power over the rules.
definitions.canonical: The conversion of economic success or political office into control of the rules that govern others.

definitions.short: Decide at the lowest competent level; escalate only when necessary.
definitions.canonical: Authority should rest at the most local level capable of performing a function well, with higher levels reserved for coordination and rights protection.

definitions.short: Citizens can see money, decisions, contracts, algorithms, and appeals — not 'trust us.'
definitions.canonical: Government whose money flows, decisions, contracts, and automated actions are visible enough that ordinary people can understand and contest them.

definitions.short: Automated government action still requires notice, explanation, and appeal.
definitions.canonical: Constitutional process rights that survive algorithmic administration.

definitions.short: Do not remove a funding path until a proven replacement exists.
definitions.canonical: The gate set that prevents fiscal redesign from destroying essential systems before COUNTABLE replacement cash exists.

definitions.short: Ability to absorb shock without cascading household catastrophe.
definitions.canonical: The capacity of households, communities, and systems to withstand disruption while preserving essential function and recovery options.

definitions.short: Maintain quality of life while responsibly resizing for a smaller population.
definitions.canonical: A place can maintain quality of life while responsibly resizing systems built for a larger population — growth is not the definition of prosperity.

definitions.short: Housing, schools, water, care, and finance keep pace when people and jobs arrive.
definitions.canonical: The ability of a growing place to expand productive and care capacity so prices do not absorb every prosperity gain.

definitions.short: Assets — human, productive, public, natural, civic, constitutional — that reach the next generation.
definitions.canonical: Capital that compounds across generations rather than being consumed as present comfort.

is_is_not_faq.a: No. Private productive property, profit, markets, and differentiated outcomes remain fundamental.
No. Markets can fail; monopoly and capture are real; government has defined protective roles.
Not by default. Public ownership is narrow and must pass strict gates.
No. Dual abolition FAILED Stage 4. COUNTABLE alternative cash today is $0.
No. It pursues human standing and meaningful capability — not equal outcomes.
No. It celebrates wealth creation and constrains conversion of wealth into unaccountable governing power.
No. Net-capability retention is not buy-local nationalism. Arkansas should trade.
The people, through constitutional government — not markets alone, not experts alone, not the richest actor.
